text.p: Iranians vote in by-elections on Friday in Iran's third largest city Isfahan and other districts where results of last year's parliamentary poll were annulled because of alleged irregularities.

Local issues have dominated campaigns to fill 22 seats of the 270-member Majlis or parliament but there has been tension between conservatives and centrist backers of President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani over a screening process that decides who is allowed to run.

Screening committees set up by the Guardian Council, a body of clerics and lawyers which oversees elections, last month approved 215 candidates from about twice as many contenders. Some approved candidates have since withdrawn, newspapers said.

Polls will open at 8 a.m. (0430 GMT) for 10 hours at more than 2,000 polling stations in 15 districts spread across nine provinces. Officials said first results would be announced about 24 hours after the stations close.

All district residents aged 15 and above can vote for the candidates, who are contesting seats left empty after the Guardian Council annulled results of two rounds of voting last March and April because of what it said were irregularities.
Some political figures and newspapers charged that the annullments -- particularly the one in Isfahan -- favoured conservatives who oppose Rafsanjani's reform policies and his centrist supporters.
The Guardian Council screens candidates for their belief in Islam and Iran's system of Islamic government, including the rule that the state is headed by a supreme spiritual leader.
Campaigning, allowed for one week up to Wednesday night, was low-key compared to last year's main poll.
But residents in Isfahan, 300 km (185 miles) south of Tehran, said walls were covered with posters and there were cases of rivals tearing up each others' flyers.

The conservatives, led by parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, maintained their Majlis majority in last year's elections. But analysts said they faced a strong minority coalition of pro-Rafsanjani centrists, radical Islamist intellectuals and labour groups.
The 22 new Majlis members' votes could be significant because of the small gap between parliament's two political blocks, analysts said.

Also at stake is momentum for presidential polls, due in May or June, in which Rafsanjani is barred from running after serving two four-year terms. Nateq-Nouri appears to be the leading candidate for the post after keeping a high media profile in the past months.

Conservative Shi'ite Moslem clerics and politicians, concerned about maintaining support for the Islamic state with its powerbase of poor and dispossessed, have slowed progress on Rafsanjani's market liberalisation policies.
The president's backers are eager to carry through reforms and focus on economic growth to overcome problems caused by an inefficient state sector and underdevelopment.
